title: What Is a Chargeback? Dispute Process and Prevention Tips
summary: Understand how credit card chargebacks work, why disputes happen, and the best practices merchants use to prevent costly reversals.
body_markdown:
You process a completely normal order, and weeks later the bank pulls the funds right back out. The buyer keeps the item, and you pay a penalty fee on top of the lost sale. Anyone asking what is a chargeback in banking is usually dealing with this exact headache. Our view: the cheapest chargeback is the one you block before funds move, because every lost dispute costs you the sale, the product, and a $20 to $100 processor fee. A few upfront changes to your checkout stop these claims from ever reaching your processor.


**TL;DR:**


- A chargeback is a forced fund reversal where banks pull disputed money directly from your account.
- Global card fraud hit $33.41 billion in 2024. Forced reversals trigger compounding penalty fees.
- Buyers have 60 days under federal law to file disputes, with some fraud cases extended to 120 days by bank policy. Missing your rebuttal deadline forfeits the funds.
- Block disputes early by updating billing descriptors, displaying return rules, and requiring CVVs.
- The Dots API natively resolves chargeback compliance and blocks disputes before funds move.


## What Is a Chargeback?


To answer what is a chargeback on a credit card, it is a forced fund reversal initiated by a consumer's issuing bank. When a cardholder disputes a transaction, their financial institution bypasses you completely. The bank pulls the money directly from your merchant account and returns it to the buyer.


Often referred to when explaining what is a chargeback in banking, this mechanism places the burden of proof entirely onto the merchant. You must assemble compelling transaction evidence to reclaim your capital before a strict card network deadline expires. If you miss that window, the forced reversal becomes permanent. You absorb both the lost sale and compounding processor penalty fees.


## The Difference Between a Chargeback and a Refund


A refund is a voluntary return of capital you control. In contrast, a chargeback transfers that control entirely to the issuing bank, which automatically withdraws the disputed funds and a penalty fee directly from your account.

## The Three Main Causes of Chargebacks


Disputes stem from three primary categories. Recognizing these triggers helps you block forced fund reversals early.


### True Fraud


Criminals use stolen card details for unauthorized purchases. The legitimate cardholder spots the charge on their statement and notifies their bank, which pulls the funds from your[payout](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-a-payout/) account to protect the victim.


### Friendly Fraud


Customers dispute valid purchases because they forget the transaction or intentionally abuse the dispute process to keep an item without paying. This type of claim forces you to submit real-time transaction logs and delivery receipts to prove the purchase was legitimate. While you assemble this evidence, the issuing bank still pulls the disputed funds and a penalty fee directly from your merchant account.


### Merchant Error


Some disputes trace back to mistakes on your own end. You might double charge a buyer, bill the wrong amount, or charge a card after a cancellation already went through. You might also ship an order late or send the wrong item entirely. Banks side with the buyer on these claims because the error is real, so your best defense is accurate order processing paired with a fast refund the moment you spot the mistake.


## How the Chargeback Process Works


The chargeback process triggers the second a buyer contacts their credit card issuer to dispute a transaction. A strict sequence controls how banks handle the funds.


### Initiation


The issuing bank reviews the complaint and assigns a standardized reason code. First, you contact their card issuer to dispute the charge. The issuer checks the claim against card network rules to confirm it qualifies. The reason code, for example a fraud code for an unauthorized transaction or a code for merchandise not received, tells you which evidence you will need to win.


### Bank Reversal


The issuer withdraws the transaction amount and a penalty fee from your acquiring bank, pulling funds directly from your account. The buyer typically receives a provisional credit while the dispute stays open, so they get their money back before any investigation finishes. Your acquiring bank debits your merchant account to cover that provisional credit plus the processor fee. On a $200 order with a $25 processor fee, $225 leaves your account before you ever get the chance to respond.


### Merchant Notification


Your processor flags the dispute, freezing the contested amount and requesting documentation. The notice lists the reason code, the disputed amount, and the response deadline you must meet. That response window is often just days, set by the card network and your processor, not weeks. You should decide right away whether to fight the dispute with evidence or accept the loss.


### Evidence Rebuttal


You must submit transaction evidence like delivery receipts or IP logs before the deadline expires. This rebuttal is often called representment, and the issuing bank expects your packet to match the reason code tied to the claim. For an item-not-received dispute, that means tracking with signed delivery confirmation, while a fraud claim calls for AVS and CVV match results plus IP logs tied to the purchase. Round out the packet with your accepted refund policy and any customer communications showing the order was legitimate. An incomplete or late packet loses by default, so assemble every document well before the deadline.


### Final Resolution


If your evidence proves validity, the bank returns your funds. If the rebuttal fails, the loss becomes permanent.


## The Financial Impact of Chargebacks on Merchants


Understanding what is a chargeback in business requires looking at the compounding financial penalties. Global payment card fraud losses reached[$33.41 billion in 2024](https://redo.com/articles/chargebacks/chargeback-statistics) . When a forced reversal occurs, the impact extends far beyond a single refunded transaction.


The trend is worsening.[Mastercard projects](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en/news-and-trends/Insights/2025/2025-global-chargebacks-outlook.html) global chargeback volume will reach 324 million transactions annually by 2028, a 24% increase from 2025. Merchants who wait to build dispute defenses will face a growing share of that volume.


Processor fees typically run $20 to $100 per dispute, proving why merchants need a clear strategy to[mitigate payment fraud](https://usedots.com/blog/mitigate-fraud-payouts/) . The issuing bank pulls both the disputed transaction amount and this penalty fee directly from your merchant account. You absorb these compounding costs on top of the lost sale. Catching criminal abuse before funds move is the only way to protect your revenue.


## Time Limits for Filing a Chargeback


Cardholders cannot dispute transactions indefinitely. A strict credit card chargeback time limit restricts this liability window. Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, consumers have[60 days from the date](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/fair_credit_billing_act_%28fcba%29) a billing statement arrives to dispute charges over $50. Once this expires, the issuing bank rejects the complaint.


Different payment methods carry different rules, and disputes like these often trace back to the same[types of payout fraud](https://usedots.com/blog/types-of-payout-fraud/) merchants see elsewhere. A debit card chargeback time limit falls under the[Electronic Fund Transfer Act](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/compliance-resources/deposit-accounts-resources/electronic-fund-transfers/electronic-fund-transfers-faqs/) , which enforces separate deadlines. Banks frequently extend these windows based on internal policies, giving buyers[up to 120 days](https://www.visa.co.uk/how-you-pay-matters/chargeback-purchase-disputes.html) in specific fraud cases.


You must track these timelines closely. Missing a merchant rebuttal deadline by a single day means you forfeit the disputed funds entirely.


## Best Practices for Preventing Chargebacks


Stopping disputes before they post protects your revenue. Proactive strategies lower your dispute ratio and catch criminal abuse before funds move.


### Clear Billing Descriptors


Buyers panic over unrecognizable bank statement names and immediately try to reverse credit card charges. Update your merchant descriptor to match your brand name, eliminating buyer confusion.


### Transparent Return Policies


Display refund rules clearly at checkout. When buyers cannot find return guidelines, they bypass support entirely. In the chargeback vs refund calculation, the math favors refunds: on a $150 order with a $30 processor fee, a chargeback costs you $180 and the merchandise, while a voluntary refund costs $150 and returns the item to stock. Make refunds the easiest path for every unhappy buyer.


### Fraud Detection Systems


Block criminal activity before transactions clear. Screen purchases for mismatched shipping details and require CVV verification. Flagging high-risk checkout behavior stops stolen card abuse from reaching your account, a tactic that also guards against common[marketplace fraud schemes](https://usedots.com/blog/marketplace-fraud-schemes/) .
